name_en: Linear-algebraic vocabulary applies to objects that are not column vectors
name_zh: 线性代数词汇不限于列向量
statement: Independence, spanning, basis and dimension are defined for elements of an arbitrary linear space; matrices, polynomials and continuous functions are legitimate 'vectors'. Nothing in these four notions refers to coordinates or to columns of numbers.
divergence: Apostol makes this the *starting point*: the ten axioms come first, V_n is only EXAMPLE 3 of twelve in 15.03, and function spaces (EXAMPLE 5-10: all functions, polynomials, C(a,b), differentiable, integrable) sit on the same page as R^n, so every later theorem is automatically a theorem about functions. Strang gets to the same place from the other end and does get there in full: 3.4 runs on columns, elimination and pivots for its first two thirds, then a named section 'Bases for Matrix Spaces and Function Spaces' actually computes non-column dimensions -- 2x2 matrices (4, with an explicit basis), n by n matrices (n^2), upper triangular (n^2/2 + n/2), diagonal (n), symmetric (n^2/2 + n/2) -- and then bases of ODE solution spaces: {x, 1} for y'' = 0, {sin x, cos x} for y'' = -y, {e^x, e^-x} for y'' = y, dimension 2 each. So the divergence is not coverage but *order and leverage*. Apostol's generality is load-bearing (his approximation theory in 15.11-15.16 runs on C(a,b), never on R^n), whereas Strang's is terminal: the matrix machinery he built (pivots, rank, R) does not apply to sin x and cos x, so the non-column bases are read off by inspection and nothing downstream in Chapter 3 uses them. Apostol pays by having no algorithm for *producing* a basis or a dimension from given data anywhere in 15.05-15.08; his single constructive algorithm in the chapter is Gram-Schmidt (15.13), and that one orthogonalizes a sequence you already have.

anchors.quote: When a theorem is deduced from the axioms of a linear space, we obtain, in one stroke, a result valid for each concrete example.
The words "independence" and "basis" and "dimension" are not at all restricted to column vectors.

name_en: Span of a set of elements
name_zh: 集合的张成
statement: The set of all finite linear combinations of the elements of a set S is a subspace, the smallest one containing S. Different sets can have the same span, so a span does not determine its generators.
divergence: Apostol builds the span bottom-up as an operator L(S) on arbitrary (possibly infinite) subsets, proves it is the smallest subspace containing S by the closure test, and must therefore also legislate L(empty) = {O}. Strang has the concept but no operator and no notation: 'span' is a verb applied to a finite list, and the object it produces is always already named as something else -- the column space or the row space of a matrix, or the solution space of an ODE. He can and does handle non-column spans (in 3.4 he names {sin x, cos x} as a basis of the solutions of y'' = -y), so the loss is not expressive power over such objects but the absence of a *term for the operation*: there is no L(S) to write down, no way to name a subspace by its generators alone before knowing what it turns out to be, and hence no way to state 'different sets may span the same subspace' as a fact about an operator being non-injective. What Strang buys instead is decidability: the pivot columns of A are a basis for C(A), computed by elimination. He also loses Apostol's empty-set convention and has to reinstate the zero space by hand, declaring the empty set a basis for Z in the last paragraph of 3.4.

anchors.quote: We call this the subspace spanned by S, or the linear span of S, and denote it by $L(S)$ .
Different sets may span the same subspace.
DEFINITION A set of vectors spans a space if their linear combinations fill the space.

name_en: Linear independence as the uniqueness of the vanishing combination
name_zh: 线性无关:零组合的唯一性
statement: A family of elements is independent when the only finite linear combination of them equal to the zero element is the one with all coefficients zero. Dependence is the existence of a single witnessing relation with some coefficient nonzero.
divergence: Apostol defines dependence first and independence as its negation, over an unordered and possibly infinite *set*; the distinctness and finiteness clauses are therefore load-bearing, and the definition applies verbatim to {1, t, t^2, ...} and to exponentials with distinct exponents. Strang defines independence first, for a finite *sequence*, and in the same breath converts it into the matrix test N(A) = {0}, i.e. into elimination. The trade is a decision procedure against a domain: Strang can settle independence of any concrete list in finitely many row operations and can never phrase the question for an infinite family; Apostol can phrase it for infinite families and must invent a fresh ad hoc argument (differentiate and evaluate at 0; a limit argument for exponentials) for each one, since he has no algorithm at all.

anchors.quote: The set $S$ is called independent if it is not dependent. In this case, for all choices of distinct elements $x_{1},\ldots ,x_{k}$ in $S$ and scalars $c_{1},\ldots ,c_{k}$ ,
DEFINITION The columns of A are linearly independent when the only solution to Ax = 0 is x = 0.
DEFINITION The sequence of vectors $v _ { 1 } , \ldots , v _ { n }$ is linearly independent if the only combination that gives the zero vector is

name_en: A family containing the zero element is dependent
name_zh: 含零元的族必相关
statement: Any family that contains the zero element is dependent, because that element alone admits a nontrivial vanishing combination. Consequently the zero element can never belong to a basis, and the empty set is the (only) basis of the zero space.
divergence: Both books reach 'the empty set is a basis for the zero space', but from opposite directions. Apostol gets it for free and in the open: independence is a universally quantified statement, so it is vacuously true of the empty set (EXAMPLE 4 of 15.07), and L(empty) is declared to be {O}; no motive is needed. Strang gets it as a closing stipulation in the last paragraph of 3.4, and the only reason he gives is 'because then linear independence is lost'. That the deeper function of the rule is to protect the dimension count -- admitting O would let a space have bases of different sizes and break dim = number of basis vectors -- is substantive but *not stated by the textbook*; it is our inference, not his sentence. So a fact that is a triviality on the axiomatic route arrives on the matrix route as an unexplained house rule.

anchors.quote: EXAMPLE 3. If $O \in S$ , then $S$ is dependent.
EXAMPLE 4. The empty set is independent.
We can never allow the zero vector into a basis, because then linear independence is lost.

name_en: Basis: an independent spanning family
name_zh: 基:独立且张成
statement: A basis of a space is a family that is both independent and spanning. The two clauses are logically independent of each other, and together they are what makes representation of every element possible and unique.
divergence: The invariant is identical; the carrier is not. Apostol's basis is a *set*, so ordering is absent and must be added later as a separate definition (ordered basis) at exactly the point where components are introduced. Strang's basis is a *sequence* from the start, because he intends to load it into the columns of a matrix, and ordering is then free. Strang's cost shows up as a warning label: because bases and matrices are so nearly identified in his notation, he has to forbid the phrases 'the dimension of a basis' and 'the basis of a matrix' outright. Apostol's cost is confined to the existence chain 15.05-15.08: there he asserts that a basis exists (Theorem 15.7a) and never produces one, whereas every Strang basis in 3.4-3.5 comes out of elimination. It is not true that Apostol never constructs anything -- 15.13 gives Gram-Schmidt, his one algorithm in the chapter, and its corollary constructs an orthogonal basis of any finite-dimensional Euclidean space. The difference is that Gram-Schmidt improves a sequence you are handed, while elimination extracts a basis from a subspace presented as a column space or a nullspace.

anchors.quote: DEFINITION. A finite set S of elements in a linear space V is called a finite basis for V if S is independent and spans V.
DEFINITION A basis for a vector space is a sequence of vectors with two properties:
Note about the language of linear algebra We never say "the rank of a space" or "the dimension of a basis" or "the basis of a matrix".

name_en: Coordinates relative to a basis exist and are unique
name_zh: 基下坐标的存在与唯一
statement: Relative to a fixed basis, every element has exactly one representation as a linear combination of the basis elements: existence comes from spanning, uniqueness from independence. Both books prove uniqueness by subtracting two representations and applying independence to the difference.
divergence: Here the two books are closest: even the proofs coincide line for line (assume two expansions, subtract, invoke independence). The only divergence is what the theorem is *for*. Apostol uses it to define the coordinate n-tuple, i.e. to justify the very notion of components, and immediately notes that the tuple depends on the ordering and not only on the basis-as-a-set. Strang states it in one line and does not build coordinates on it, because his vectors already arrive as coordinate tuples in R^n -- the theorem he actually needs later is not 'coordinates exist' but 'A is invertible from row space to column space'. So the theorem that founds Apostol's coordinates is, for Strang, a remark he can afford to spend two sentences on.

anchors.quote: The coefficients in this equation determine an n-tuple of numbers $(c_{1},\ldots,c_{n})$ that is uniquely determined by x.
There is one and only one way to write v as a combination of the basis vectors.

name_en: Any two bases of the same space have the same number of elements
name_zh: 同一空间的任两个基元素个数相同
statement: Two bases of one space cannot have different sizes. This is the theorem that makes 'dimension' a well-defined function of the space rather than of a chosen basis.
divergence: Same statement, and both prove it by a two-sided counting squeeze, but the engine differs. Apostol routes it through Theorem 15.5 ('k+1 elements of the span of an independent k-set are dependent'), a pure consequence of the axioms, applied twice by symmetry. Strang writes the w's as combinations of the v's, i.e. as a matrix product VA with A short-and-wide, and then quotes his own 'm < n forces dependent columns'. Strang's proof is shorter and constructive but it is a proof *about matrices*: it presupposes that the vectors can be stacked into columns, so as written it does not cover matrix spaces or function spaces -- for which he only asserts the analogue. Apostol's proof needs no representation and therefore certifies dim of the polynomials of degree <= n directly.

anchors.quote: THEOREM 15.6. Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional linear space. Then every finite basis for $V$ has the same number of elements.
If $\pmb { v } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { v } _ { m }$ and $w _ { 1 } , \ldots , w _ { n }$ are both bases for the same vector space, then $m = n$

name_en: Dimension of a space versus rank of a matrix
name_zh: 空间的维数与矩阵的秩
statement: Dimension is the common size of all bases of a space. Rank is an attribute of a matrix, equal to the number of pivots, and it happens to equal the dimension of that matrix's column space and of its row space. The two words are not interchangeable: only one of them is defined for a space and only one is defined for a matrix.
divergence: Apostol has dimension and no rank whatsoever: the word does not occur in Chapter 15. The chain 15.05-15.07 is metric-free and representation-free, and 'dim V = n' is all he ever needs, so he can assign a dimension to C(a,b)'s polynomial subspaces without computing anything. Strang has both, and the entire content of 3.5 is the bridge between them. That bridge is Strang-only and has no Apostol counterpart at all: the Rank Theorem (independent columns = independent rows), the Counting Theorem, and the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra part 1 (all four subspace dimensions of one matrix at once) are statements about a matrix, so they are not shared invariants but Strang's own additions -- Apostol's vocabulary cannot formulate them, having no matrix and hence no four subspaces. What rank buys Strang is arithmetic: r + (n - r) = n pins those four dimensions simultaneously. What it costs is the confusion he then has to police explicitly, since a space has no rank and a matrix has no dimension.

anchors.quote: DEFINITION. If a linear space V has a basis of n elements, the integer n is called the dimension of V.
The main theorem in this chapter connects rank and dimension. The rank of a matrix is the number of pivots. The dimension of a subspace is the number of vectors in a basis.
Rank Theorem: The number of independent columns =the number of independent rows

name_en: What independence of the generating family is used for
name_zh: 生成族独立性的用处
statement: Independence of a generating family is exactly the condition that makes the representation of an element by that family unique. In matrix form it is full column rank, equivalently a trivial nullspace, equivalently invertibility of A-transpose-A.
divergence: Apostol cashes independence for uniqueness of components (15.08) and, separately, for the extension and exchange results of 15.07; he does not develop it into a battery of equivalent tests. Strang turns it into exactly that: all columns are pivot columns, no free variables, N(A) = {0}, at most one solution of Ax = b, and (in 4.2) A-transpose-A invertible so that x-hat is unique. Every link in that chain is a statement about the *representing matrix*, not about the subspace, which is why Apostol cannot state any of them. The price Strang pays becomes visible only when independence fails: the projection p onto the column space still exists and is still unique, but the coefficient vector x-hat is not -- a distinction that has no counterpart in Apostol, who never separates an element of S from its coefficient tuple.

anchors.quote: But since the basis elements are independent, this implies $c_{i}=d_{i}$ for each i

name_en: The bilinear pairing that carries length and angle
name_zh: 承载长度与角度的配对
statement: Geometry is imported into a linear space by a pairing of two elements that is conjugate-symmetric (simply symmetric in the real case), positive-definite, and linear in the first argument while conjugate-linear in the second (simply bilinear in the real case). Length is the square root of the pairing of an element with itself, and orthogonality is the vanishing of the pairing.
divergence: Apostol axiomatises the pairing and then exhibits several on one and the same space -- the component sum, a weighted sum, an integral, a weighted integral -- so 'orthogonal' is always relative to a chosen product, and the sentence 'cos nx is orthogonal to sin mx' becomes literally the same sentence as 'e_1 is orthogonal to e_2'. Strang fixes one pairing and writes it as v-transpose-w, which is not a neutral choice: the transpose then does double duty as the adjoint, so A-transpose generates the other two of his four subspaces and A-transpose-A appears as the normal-equation matrix. That single notation is what makes his whole chapter computable, and it is also what hides the arbitrariness of the pairing: nothing in his notation suggests that an integral could take the place of the sum, and function approximation is therefore deferred out of the chapter entirely.

anchors.quote: In a general linear space, we write $(x, y)$ instead of $x \cdot y$ for inner products, and we define the product axiomatically rather than by a specific formula.
This example shows that there may be more than one inner product in a given linear space.
Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero: $\boldsymbol { v } \boldsymbol { \cdot w } = \boldsymbol { v } ^ { \mathrm { T } } \boldsymbol { w } = \boldsymbol { 0 }$ .

name_en: Orthogonality defined as a vanishing pairing
name_zh: 正交即配对为零
statement: Two elements are orthogonal when their pairing is zero. The zero element is orthogonal to everything, and it is the only element orthogonal to itself -- a fact that comes from positive definiteness and is used as a uniqueness device in both books.
divergence: Identical invariant, and both books use the self-orthogonality fact for the same purpose -- as the step that forces a difference to vanish (Apostol in the uniqueness half of Theorem 15.15, Strang in showing that two orthogonal subspaces meet only at 0, and again in showing that x_r is determined by Ax). The divergence is in where the fact is grounded. Apostol derives it from the positivity axiom, so it holds in any Euclidean space including C(a,b): a continuous function orthogonal to itself is the zero function. Strang states it as a property of vectors in R^n, obtained from v-transpose-v = 0. His version is a special case, and because it is stated for vectors rather than for the pairing, the transfer to functions is not available to him inside these sections.

anchors.quote: The zero element is orthogonal to every element of V; it is the only element orthogonal to itself.
If a vector v is orthogonal to itself then v is the zero vector.
When a vector is in two orthogonal subspaces, it must be zero. It is perpendicular to itself.

name_en: Pythagorean identity for orthogonal summands
name_zh: 正交分量的勾股恒等式
statement: If two elements are orthogonal, the squared norm of their sum is the sum of their squared norms, because the cross terms in the expansion vanish.
divergence: Apostol states it only as a rider to the orthogonal decomposition theorem (15.17), applied to the pair s and s-perp; it is a corollary, not a tool, and he uses it once more inside the proof of the approximation theorem. Strang puts it in position 1 of the section header, before anything else, and immediately reads it off the right triangle b-p-e; for him it is the visual justification of why the perpendicular foot is the closest point. Same identity, opposite pedagogical direction: Apostol derives it from orthogonality and then derives minimality from it algebraically, whereas Strang draws minimality from the picture and uses the identity to confirm it. The consequence is that Strang's version is bound to a right triangle in R^m and does not obviously carry to functions; Apostol's carries with no change of wording.

anchors.quote: the remaining terms being zero since $s$ and $s^{\perp}$ are orthogonal. This proves (15.17).

name_en: Being orthogonal to a whole set, and the perp of a set
name_zh: 与整个集合正交,以及集合的垂空间
statement: An element is orthogonal to a set when it is orthogonal to every member of the set. The collection of all such elements is a subspace, and being orthogonal to a set is the same as being orthogonal to its span.
divergence: Apostol defines S-perp for an *arbitrary subset* S and states that it is a subspace 'whether or not S itself is one', leaving the verification as a simple exercise rather than proving it; that generality is what licenses him to form the perp of a mere list of generators, which is the step the proof in 15.15 needs (he checks orthogonality against basis elements only, then upgrades to the span). Strang defines the perp only of a subspace V, and does so after he already knows the dimension count, so his perp always arrives paired with its partner in a complement pair. Strang's concrete gain is large -- 'the nullspace consists of the vectors perpendicular to the rows' is literally the equation Ax = 0 read row by row, which no abstract statement can give -- but he cannot form the perp of a generating list as a separate object, and he needs r + (n - r) = n, i.e. elimination, to know that the perp is exactly the row space and not something larger.

anchors.quote: An element in V is said to be orthogonal to S if it is orthogonal to every element of S.
It is a simple exercise to verify that $S^{\perp}$ is a subspace of V, whether or not S itself is one.
DEFINITION The orthogonal complement of a subspace V contains every vector that is perpendicular to V.

name_en: Orthogonal pair of subspaces versus orthogonal complement
name_zh: 正交子空间对 vs 正交补
statement: The name 'orthogonal complement' is reserved for the case where the orthogonal set is taken against a subspace, and in that case the subspace and its complement together exhaust the ambient space. Mutual orthogonality of two subspaces on its own forces only that they intersect in the zero element.
divergence: The shared invariant is only the naming rule plus exhaustion. The *contrast* between mutual orthogonality and complementarity is Strang-only: he isolates it as an explicit trap and spends a counterexample on it (two walls of a room look perpendicular but are not orthogonal subspaces; two planes in R^3 can never be orthogonal complements, because the dimensions must add up), and he can make the point sharply precisely because he has dimension arithmetic. The weaker relation therefore exists as a named object for him -- orthogonal subspaces, whose only forced consequence is that they meet in the zero vector -- and not for Apostol. On Apostol's route the distinction cannot arise: he only ever forms S-perp of a given S, and S together with S-perp is a complement pair by construction (Theorem 15.15), so he needs neither the name nor the warning. Apostol pays with a silent gap -- a reader of 15.14 alone gets no warning that 'mutually orthogonal' is weaker than 'complementary' -- while Strang pays by needing the finite-dimensional count to say anything at all.

anchors.quote: In case S is a subspace, then $S^{\perp}$ is called the orthogonal complement of S.
Example 2 Two walls look perpendicular but those two subspaces are not orthogonal!
Those pairs of subspaces are not only orthogonal, they are orthogonal complements.

name_en: Unique splitting of an element along a subspace and its perp
name_zh: 元素沿子空间与其垂空间的唯一分解
statement: Given a subspace S of a space with a pairing, and provided S is finite-dimensional (Apostol) or the ambient space is finite-dimensional (Strang), every element of the ambient space is the sum of one element of S and one element of S-perp, and this splitting is unique. Uniqueness follows because the difference of two such splittings lies in both S and S-perp, hence is orthogonal to itself.
divergence: Same theorem, incompatible hypotheses. Apostol needs only that S be finite-dimensional -- the ambient V may be infinite-dimensional, which is exactly what lets him apply the theorem to C(0, 2pi) with S a space of trigonometric polynomials. His existence proof runs through a finite orthonormal basis of S, so Gram-Schmidt (15.13) is a genuine prerequisite. Strang works in R^n and gets the splitting from Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem, which he obtains from the dimension count r + (n - r) = n produced by elimination; no orthonormal basis is constructed anywhere. Strang's version therefore yields something Apostol's does not -- that A restricted from row space to column space is invertible, the germ of the pseudoinverse -- while Apostol's version applies where Strang's count is unavailable.

anchors.quote: Then every element x in V can be represented uniquely as a sum of two elements, one in S and one in $S^{\perp}$ .
$N ( A )$ is the orthogonal complement of the row space $C ( A ^ { \mathrm { T } } )$
The point of "complements" is that every x can be split into a row space component

name_en: Projection along a single nonzero direction
name_zh: 沿单个非零方向的投影
statement: For a nonzero direction y, the projection of x along y is the multiple of y whose coefficient is the pairing of x with y divided by the pairing of y with itself. The remainder x minus that multiple is orthogonal to y.
divergence: The formula is character-for-character the same object -- coefficient = pairing with the direction over the direction's self-pairing. The roles are reversed. For Apostol this is an *internal step of an algorithm*: it is named only in passing while explaining Gram-Schmidt, and at that point he has not yet claimed it minimises any distance (minimality waits for 15.16). For Strang it is the *foundation of the chapter*: it is introduced as the closest-point problem, the error is shown perpendicular at once, and it is immediately packaged as a rank-one matrix P = a a-transpose over a-transpose-a with P squared equal to P. Strang thereby gains the operator viewpoint -- projection as a matrix acting on all b at once, and I - P projecting onto the perpendicular complement -- which Apostol never forms, since without a representation he has no object 'the projection map'.

anchors.quote: is called the projection of x along y. In the Gram-Schmidt process (15.15), we construct the element $y_{r+1}$ by subtracting from $x_{r+1}$ the projection
The projection of b onto the line through a is the vector $p = { \widehat { x } } a = { \frac { a ^ { \mathrm { T } } b } { a ^ { \mathrm { T } } a } } a$
When P projects onto one subspace, $I - P$ projects onto the perpendicular subspace.

name_en: Projection of an element onto a finite-dimensional subspace
name_zh: 元素在有限维子空间上的投影
statement: Given a finite-dimensional subspace S and an element x of the ambient space, the projection of x on S is the unique element p of S such that x minus p is orthogonal to S. It is the S-component of the orthogonal splitting of x, and it does not depend on how S is presented.
divergence: This is the sharpest trade in the two chapters, and it is a trade of *hypothesis against computation*. Apostol defines the projection as the sum of the projections of x along the elements of an ORTHONORMAL basis of S. The definition is therefore unusable until such a basis exists, which is precisely why Gram-Schmidt and Theorem 15.14 must come first (15.13 before 15.14); in exchange the formula is a bare sum of pairings, requires no inversion, no determinant and no independence hypothesis beyond that of a basis, and it reads identically in C(a,b), where it becomes the Fourier/Legendre partial sum. Strang starts from an arbitrary INDEPENDENT list a_1,...,a_n -- no orthogonality assumed, hence no Gram-Schmidt needed at this point in the book -- and pays for it twice: he must impose orthogonality as n equations, A-transpose(b - A x-hat) = 0, and then SOLVE the resulting normal equation A-transpose-A x-hat = A-transpose-b, which forces him to prove separately that A-transpose-A is invertible exactly when the columns are independent. Net: Apostol front-loads the cost into constructing a basis and gets a closed formula; Strang front-loads nothing and pays with a linear system plus an invertibility theorem every single time. Strang's compensation is the projection matrix P = A(A-transpose-A)^{-1}A-transpose, an object valid for all b simultaneously and characterisable by P-transpose = P, P squared = P -- which Apostol's basis-dependent sum never becomes.

name_en: The residual is orthogonal to the approximating subspace
name_zh: 残差与逼近子空间正交
statement: The difference between an element and its projection on a subspace is orthogonal to that entire subspace. This single condition characterises the projection and is what both books use to identify it.
divergence: The logical direction is opposite. Apostol DEFINES s by a formula and then VERIFIES that x - s is orthogonal to each basis element, upgrading to all of S by linearity; orthogonality is a checked consequence. Strang IMPOSES orthogonality as the defining requirement -- the n right angles are the n equations -- and derives the formula from it; orthogonality is the input. Strang also names the residual twice over: as the error vector e = b - p, and as an element of N(A-transpose), the left nullspace. That second name is pure presentation artifact: it exists only because his subspace happens to be the column space of a matrix A, so 'orthogonal to S' can be rewritten as 'annihilated by A-transpose'. Apostol has no A, so he has one name where Strang has two, and Strang's second name is the one that connects the residual to his four-subspace picture.

anchors.quote: Therefore $s^\perp$ is orthogonal to every element in $S$ , which means that $s^\perp \in S^\perp$ .

The left nullspace is important in projections. That nullspace of $A ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ contains the error vector

name_en: The projection is the unique nearest element of the subspace
name_zh: 投影是子空间中唯一的最近元
statement: Among all elements of a finite-dimensional subspace S, the projection of x on S minimises the distance to x, and it is the only minimiser. The proof splits x - t into the orthogonal parts (x - s) and (s - t) and applies the Pythagorean identity.
divergence: For Apostol minimality is a THEOREM, stated separately in its own section 15.15, with a proof and an explicit uniqueness clause ('the equality sign holds if and only if t = s'); the projection was defined algebraically first, and its optimality had to be earned. For Strang minimality is the DEFINITION -- 'the closest vector p in S' is how projection onto a subspace is introduced in the section header -- so there is nothing left to prove, and no uniqueness clause is stated anywhere in 4.2. That is the whole cost of his choice: he never has to prove the approximation theorem, and he also never gets a statement of it, so within 4.1-4.2 the fact that the minimiser is unique is carried only by the geometry of the picture. The application layers then diverge completely: Apostol's theorem instantiates to Fourier partial sums and Legendre approximation of continuous functions, both of which are the same theorem with a different pairing; Strang's flows into least squares fitting of data, and he defers function approximation out of the chapter.

name_en: Minimising a squared residual is a projection problem
name_zh: 最小化平方残差就是投影问题
statement: When an element cannot be represented exactly by the available generators, the best representation in the norm induced by the pairing is obtained by projecting onto the subspace they span. The unsolvable exact problem is thus replaced by a solvable orthogonality condition.
divergence: The two books arrive from opposite motivations. Apostol's motive is APPROXIMATION THEORY: x is a continuous function, S is a space of polynomials or trigonometric polynomials, and the question 'which element of S is nearest' is posed for its own sake, with no equation in sight. Strang's motive is an UNSOLVABLE SYSTEM: b lies outside the column space, so Ax = b has no solution, and the least-squares problem is the salvage operation -- his 4.1 announces the error vector b - Ax as living in N(A-transpose) before projections are even defined. Consequence: Apostol never mentions equations, so a reader of ch15 alone would not know that this theory solves overdetermined systems; Strang, inside 4.1-4.2, has no norm on functions and hence no way to pose approximation of a function, so the entire polynomial/Fourier half of the subject is invisible from his side of the alignment.

anchors.quote: Given an element x in V, to determine an element in S whose distance from x is as small as possible.
It contains the error $e = b - A x$ in the "least-squares" solution. Least squares is the key application of linear algebra in this chapter.

name_en: Solutions of a homogeneous linear condition form a subspace
name_zh: 齐次线性条件的解集是子空间
statement: The set of solutions of a homogeneous linear condition is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, hence a subspace; the solutions of the corresponding inhomogeneous condition are one particular solution plus that subspace.
divergence: Apostol exhibits this as one example among twelve, for a second-order homogeneous differential equation, and notes only that the zero on the right-hand side is essential -- the inhomogeneous set fails the closure axioms. He gets the differential-equation case into the same theory as R^n for free, and gets no method: he asserts that the solution space has dimension 2 without solving anything. Strang makes exactly this decomposition the goal of section 3.3 and supplies the algorithm: eliminate on the augmented matrix, read the particular solution off d, read the n - r special solutions off the free columns. He gains a complete procedure for matrices and pays by never once applying it to a differential equation, so the shared structure -- that both are the same coset statement -- is left for the reader to notice.

anchors.quote: The set of solutions of a nonhomogeneous differential equation does not satisfy the closure axioms.
Figure 3.3: Complete solution = one particular solution + all nullspace solutions.

name_en: With the right number of elements, one basis property implies the other
name_zh: 元素个数正确时,基的一个性质推出另一个
statement: In a space of dimension n, any n independent elements already span it, and hence form a basis. Only one of the two basis clauses has to be checked once the count is known to be right.
divergence: Apostol states it as Theorem 15.7(b) for an abstract space of dimension n and delegates the proof to Chapter 12, so on his route it is a labour-saving corollary of the counting theory and nothing more. Strang states both halves (n independent vectors span; n spanning vectors are independent), notes that it holds in any vector space, and then immediately re-reads it as a statement about an n by n matrix being invertible -- which converts an existence claim into a determinant/elimination test. That conversion is the gain and the limit at once: it is a decision procedure in R^n, and it is unavailable for the matrix and function spaces he has just admitted, where his own general formulation still holds but cannot be checked by his methods. Apostol's version, by contrast, applies to a space of polynomials verbatim, and he uses it in 15.11 to conclude that n nonzero orthogonal elements are a basis.

anchors.quote: (b) Any set of n independent elements is a basis for V.
Any n independent vectors in $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ must span $\mathbf { R } ^ { n }$ . So they are a basis.
Starting with the correct number of vectors, one property of a basis produces the other.
